power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Another strength was the great number and variety of independent variables studied, contrasting with precedents' limitation to few variables; [1] [2] [3] [4] [8] [9] [10] [11] [12] [13] 16, 19, 21, [34] [35] [36] [37] [38] [39] most commonly, in order, sex, area of practice, domestic or international qualification, practise length and type, allegations, age, and race, focusing on characteristics that are nonmodifiable for risk mitigation. Our richer context helped us pinpoint which factors predominantly related to decisions and, just as crucially, which were not. This addressed many live questions -only a few discussed at length. Nonetheless, as in any similar design, there still could be important unidentified latent variables. Some are anecdotally reported to affect akin decisions, but remain hard to measure and therefore analyse quantitatively. For example: acceptance of accountability, contrition or insight, candour, and remediation. 20, 40 Large sample sizes enabled us to study rare but important factors -like conviction or qualifying in certain specialties. Also, to strongly suggest that factors with non-significant adjusted ORs were unrelated to decision outcomes, e.g. sexual orientation or religion. However, large samples complicate the interpretation of hypothesis-testing results. Especially for factors with low but significant adjusted effect sizes. For example, a desirable statistical power of ∼ 80 % for the association of being Asian and being investigated at triage (OR 1.19, or an expected probability of investigation increased by two percentage points, from the average marginal effect), required 70 % of the sample used by our triage model (n = 25, 679; post-hoc simulation drawing random samples without replacement). Large-sample requirements like these question the reliability of akin small-effect-size associations, despite statistical significance -and support interpreting such associations as artefacts of working with large samples.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.
